game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
About the game Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You, I can say that this game is one of the most thought provoking and immersive experiences I have had in a long time. The game takes place in a dystopian world where the government has implemented a surveillance system to monitor every aspect of its citizens' lives.

As a player, YOU are tasked with being the "investigator" who must review and analyze the information gathered by the Orwell System to uncover potential threats to society. However, it is up to you to determine what information is relevant and what is not, and every decision you make has consequences.

The game makes you feel like you have actual power over people's lives, and the experience of constantly analyzing data and making decisions about what information to act on or ignore makes the whole experience feel very intense and immersive .

The game's graphics and sound design are also excellent, bringing the world of Orwell to life in vivid detail. The characters are well developed, the dialogues captivating and thought-provoking.

Overall, Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is an excellent game that offers players a unique and immersive experience. It challenges us to think about the consequences of our actions and the ethics of surveillance in a society that values freedom and privacy. If you like narrative games that make you think, then this is definitely worth checking out.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is a good opportunity to have a opinion on modern day communications. There are a high possibility for the methods used in the game to solve puzzles are real.

It's nice for chilling, laying back and resting. Everything happens immediately so you won't wait for something to happen. 

Just mute the game music and play a song on Youtube, Spotify, Soundcloud... Just don't play in-game music if you wanna chill and play it for a while.

There are a couple negatives of the game, at least in my opinion.
- Music choices are not that good, it's not what it should be in that chill game. I know, the context... But still, it should be a bit relaxing.
- Puzzles are going a bit... Complicated after some time. Especially on Part 4. You literally have to take a look at everything you have to find hints, and this is REALLY annoying. I bet i spent 25% of my gameplay time on that stupid thing. It becomes boring.

Cons are enough, pros are:
+ As I mentioned above, you can just chill and do whatever you want.
+ I like the way they included  small jokes in-game. They are enough, and if you play it non-stop, they'll take your boredom.
+ Some events are random. And you can prevent some events to hapen by hiding informations.
+ Easy to play, you'll get used to it within a couple of minutes. Nothing is complicated, except the one i mentioned on cons.

Would I pay? No. Get it when it's free.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The creation of the internet is the most technological advance tool mankind has ever made, right next to toilets. With the modern age of technology we have today, the effects on our lives stack up as the age-old question Security vs. Freedom comes into the debate again.  I am talking about a game where it tackles the subject on privacy issues which is Orwell. There will be a spoiler section on the comments to give my personal thoughts on some episodes. I will give an analytical review of this game and give in my two cents if this plays well as it was intended. 

[h1]CHECKING YOUR ID[/h1]

You play as Snowden-I MEAN the investigator, you work for the government and try a new technology called Orwell. You checked on people’s devices and try to add data chunks that matter on a case you are specifically working on. To be frank, in the first episode I was intrigued by the concept of the machine, it felt the game was really inspired by the true story of Edward Snowden about the CIA scandal. Now, the difference from the actual real event and the game is that the game focus on only the investigator and your co-worker trying to solve this case together. You the investigator only see the dirty secrets while your advisor Symes only advice you on your next tasks or comment on your search. I will explain a bit more detail but it will have to be in the spoiler section on why Orwell works like that.

[h1]BACKGROUND CHARACTERS AND STORY[/h1]

I have to cut a lot to avoid spoilers so I will give you a summary of the story but will give you how the characters and their world behave. The story is interesting for how it was trying to show the concept of privacy. I absolutely love how each character from the profiles you investigate shows a unique dialogue from each text you read from different characters. They feel almost exactly like how people should talk especially on the internet. When you read each email, phone calls etc. you can picture actual people having a real conversation which is great! It never made you feel like the dialogue felt artificial or fake, like adults “trying” to sound what people would say on the internet. I also love how they try to implement how people would sound like on the comment sections and insert memes along the way. 

The art style is another unique aspect of the game of how it shows a polygonal art style look. Most of the faces are fine though some were not as quite good in certain looks like some faces of the characters you profile are a bit strange with their beady eyes or mouth. The music is quite good giving you a sense of futuristic vibe to it while also gives you a dread feeling where certain events happen during your case. You even have one shot whatever you send data chunks to Symes and you can’t go back to it even exit the game won’t do. Whatever you send to Symes will affect the characters that you are working on the case. Which now I will talk about the actual meat of the review, the concept of the game and the driving point of Orwell.

[h1] THE CHOICE IS YOURS[/h1]

The focus of what the developers are getting at is the whole anti-surveillance vs. freedom. The story hints you that the Nation (that is the country of this game) is trying to add more cameras after the safety bill was passed and some foreign problem that led to mass immigration, based on what the articles within the game said. The game even tried to give you signs that you are “supposedly” working for the bad guy and that the group that you were assigned to follow name [i]Thought[/i] is the good guys because they believe in Freedom of Speech and you are trying to incriminate them. How exactly you are incriminating them is because of how Orwell is set up to be. Orwell is a super-computer that analyze information and even interpret the information for you to post it. Unfortunately, because of how Orwell acts according to its programming it will translate the language the program will find it logical. Which leads to falsify the context that was given if you don’t read their messages clearly because remember, only you know the truth and Symes is only there as your advisor so he won’t know the full context of your side of the truth, only Orwell.  That is why it can be easy for people to get arrested just because Symes read what you send base on Orwell translated. Is this good?

 Well at first I almost had a problem with It because why the developers put it that way, but later as I finished the game I realized this was purposefully done this way and it was the right call. The purpose of their message is that people have way too much confidence of a machine to do their jobs for you they forgot how machines can be the dumbest tools for interpreting human language which they probably will never understand unless you are human. This is why in real life there are moderators to keep track of reports of people saying certain stuff. Bots can detect it but when humans actually read the context of their side of the story the problem is fix. The game did a great job of showing how humans rely on Orwell too much, but what I’m most impress is why they design the game to make it only you see the whole truth. 

In my playthrough I played the game like it was real life, I pretend I actually worked for the government and I role-play as an investigator, although sometimes I break my role to send certain data chunks that have nothing to do with the case but to pull Symes hair on certain funny comments. Anyway, when you sit down and do your “job” to be the eye on everyone’s business, not to joke around I felt pressure on taking the responsibility on sending people’s privacy, even if it means breaking some moral codes for the good of saving lives. I somehow felt like a god knowing people’s secrets and manipulate their lives on sending whatever data it comes and I send that data to Symes so that he take action to do something of this person. I can see why having this kind of power is utter madness to have, but at the same time is it really crazy to have this power?

 The game gives you a clear sense of black and white of giving you choices to follow, either be pro-government by pleasing them everything you send or follow your own thoughts of which is good and bad. Certainly, nobody here is good at least for the group [i]Thought[/i], I wish Symes would talk more of his stance of the government trying to make people safe like he would talk about how certain parts of giving up freedom for security is good even if they don’t understand. This would create an even more dilemma which the game has but certain parts fail which leads to my last discussion. 

How it handles the 1984 concepts. I felt they only scratch the surface of what it truly means for giving up your freedom. [i]Thought[/i] members tell you how bad cameras but they don’t know how the cameras are being used, they just say is bad because of privacy reasons. One member says they love the freedom of speech but at the same time I don’t see the government censoring their citizenships, maybe their newspaper but nothing more am I missing something? I heard they have immigration problem so why not show more articles showing the effects of the safety bill. Are they discriminate more by taking away their privacy than the Nation’s citizens?

 Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation?  These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. To me, it felt like a basic philosophy lesson about Orwellian which does not go as deep as I thought.  

In the end is still a great game to start with the season, the concept is interesting and even the certain parts of the game felt too real of how our world functions in terms of responding of cameras everywhere. This game deserves a 7/10! Recommend for a good short time experience for a fan of dystopian settings.

Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation? These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. To me, it felt like a basic philosophy lesson about Orwellian which does not go as deep as I thought. In the end is still a great game to start with the season, the concept is interesting and even the certain parts of the game felt too real of how our world functions in terms of responding of cameras everywhere. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Fantastic game, I can't praise it enough. Solid story, solid characters and character progression, appealing art style, and perfect general pacing. The soundtrack, works perfectly for it- being that it's essentially a solid, subtle repeat throughout the entire game really makes those times where it picks up stand out and feel that much more important.  I really, really hope to see more from this company. And, admittedly, would love it if this premise is revisited in some way. This is the best game I've played in a long, long time. Exactly what I've been looking for. I just couldn't stop playing. I'm kind of sad that I've completely finished it. 

Issues; 
Some of the dialogue becomes a bit broken depending on your choices. Oftentimes Symes and Delacroix mentioned information that I'd intentionally not given them, later on in the story. This only really becomes noticeable on replay-but it could be worked on. Nothing like this will ever be perfect--I'm never going to seriously complain about a choice game having little issues like this. There's just too much that would have to go into a game with so many variants it to make it possible. 
There were a few lingering spelling/grammatical errors, which, given the nature of the game (Internet, instant messaging/texting), didn't really bother me all that much. (Such as Harrison tried to "fell" instead of flee.) I see these things on real articles, it's no different.
There are some bugs present, but, they're clearly being revised and, honestly, aren't game-breaking at this point.

My personal ideas; I believe there could be a little work done on the pacing of the listener- real-time DOES make it all that much more immersive, but, when it comes to replayabilty, and just the general idea of it most likely having an adult player-base, who may only have an hour or so to play before going back to their day-to-day, I feel like there should be...maybe an additional option in the settings to modify speed or..something? It's easier, and more fulfilling to put a game down for a session if you feel you were able to hit a certain level of 'achievement.' You know, the pleasure centers of the brain and all. Maybe if it were simply a more fluid letter-by-letter or syllabalic instead of by completion of a word? I don't know. 
The only other thing I could possibly suggest, would be for, if ever this title is revisited or turned into a 'series' of sorts, that it be a little more flexible? The ability to freely investigate more than is necessary--even additional people. Perhaps just in a casual sense aside from the story, since there is a necessary feeling of a 'time pinch' in the game itself. I think a lot of the audience are people like me who just like to dig, so the chance to just..index on a larger scale would be quite entertaining. 
And, lastly, the ability to generate more datachunks? This could be messy territory, though. I think this would fall into the 'would require too much forethought to ever be possible' category, but it's an idea nontheless. The system is automated, clearly, but, the evaluator should have an option to deem other things appropriate for investigation. I know there were a few things that I would have loved to have flagged that just weren't an option.

My apologies, I'm just VERY excited and passionate about this title. Guys, play it!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- The game brings awareness to important social problems: surveillance and totalitarianism
- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible


Cons:
- Lack of depth in decision. The game is basically linear, except the ending which is a binary moral choice. No replay value.
- Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics.
- The conflict system makes no sense and works against realisticity. How in the world can the system predict that something is in conflict with an unknown data chunk? A conflict should only be shown when both data chunks are known. 
- Phone calls wait for you to tap, such as everything in this game. No time pressure or feeling of urgency.
- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.




This is not a bad game by any means. It's just always frustrating when I see one of these "choices matter" games where there's clearly a certain path you're encouraged to take and you really aren't free to do things your own way.

While I had pretty high expectations for this game after coming off a Hacknet binge, I just feel as though the game is trying to pretend to be something it's not. Just market the game for what it is, a linear narrative experience.

I'm very aware that since I did not finish the game my perspective is limited to what I played, but what I played I did not enjoy, so I cannot reccomend this game.

TL;DR: This game is a very and hand-holdy linear story based experience while it is advertised to be a sort of detective

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass. 

The good - 
Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot. 
The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable. 

The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs.  There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer. 

Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice. 

At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue. 

I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game. 

The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) 
If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned.


There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. 

Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, 
"Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." 
and this narrative missed that promise.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]: The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. review_text_raw:
I've been wanting to write a short but to the point review for this game. Mostly because I rarely finish any games in one go. 

Orwell is [b]NOT[/b] going to WOW you. It's not mindblowing, mind you. It will, however, keep you intrigued once you decide to give it a try. 

[u]What's it about?[/u]

It's heavily influenced by the reveals of Edward Snowden. It's about working in the NSA and uncovering personal data in order to get to the truth. It's about whether or not as people we'd sacrifice our "freedom" or our "safety". Overall, an interesting premise.

[u]Right. It's a game, so what's the gameplay like?[/u]

The "game" consists of reading a lot of text and putting certain bits of it together in order to progress to the next chapters. It doesn't sound too engaging but once you start reading through it, it is able to drag you into its universe. There are multiple endings and choices where you need to choose what to reveal for the people you gather information yourself. 

[u]Multiple choices. Does that mean there's a lot of replayability?[/u]

Well, once you get to the conclusion, you sort of feel fulfilled, hence why many of the reviewers of this game have a few hours of gametime. [b]BUT[/b] I think you can easily play the game a second time to do a few things differently. There is some replayability potential.

Good soundtrack, interesting premise, amusing characters, nice artstyle, engaging storyline. I strongly recommend this game if you want something different.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[i]Orwell[/i] is an episodic thriller involving the vulnerabilities of social media and easy access to critical digital information. You play as an employee of an NSA-like private government cyber-security agency called "Orwell", of course, named after George Orwell, and peep into your suspects' lives as you dig around for information that could tell if they are involved in anything that could put the lives of innocents in peril. The game is completely story-oriented, and at times, even choice-driven. 

[h1]Story:[/h1]

It's a thriller that follows the episode template like the [i]Telltale Games[/i], played as if you're a guy who's logged into his computer. Everything you do, see, or read is like as if you're logged into a computer. The story has a few interesting characters to read about, to peep into their lives and see just how much information you can dig up on them, and see how connected they are altogether. At times, you'll come across plot twists, and other kinds of ways the story could put you off with how you applied your actions by considering what you just saw right then first-hand, i.e., there may be more than meets the eye here. As the story progresses, the story gets deeper and darker, and your decisions will have to be considered more carefully. Sometimes, even the terms or choices given to you are there just to put you off. 

To me, I felt it drained down a bit when the whole plot unfolded, but it was pretty good overall. I haven't played the game extensively yet to see how many endings I could get, but there are indeed multiple endings. I don't dislike the endings that happen to you based on your choices. But the part of the story that you cannot change - the [b]huge[/b] plot twist - well, I didn't like it much. 

But more importantly, this game shows us just how exposed we are to everyone, and just how oblivious people are these days about this fact. It's pretty sci-fi, but who's to know that this could be our reality in a few years, give or take? We're slowly stumbling our way to a more surveilled future in which, you could say, we are going to live in an almost-communist digital world, where every singly word we type in the webs is taken for granted, and smeared on us as if we have anything troublesome to show for it. Hell, we go "Sorry, NSA" at times. So, in a way, we're just enjoying a false form of freedom. I could go into detail with how this is both good and bad, but this is only a game review, so... moving on. 

[h1]Visuals:[/h1]

The game looks like the people in it gave their own photos, and then they just used a heavily modified version of that Prisma app to convert it all to make it look like as it is. It's not bad. But, it kinda takes away the realism of it. I dunno if I could say it sits well with the tone of the game. I don't think it does. But, it's visually appealing. 

[h1]Mechanics & Gameplay:[/h1]

There's very little to no mechanics. Having the whole investigative thing in the game, it surely  calls for implementing the use of the keyboard. The devs could've considered adding search terms and stuff, but sadly, this mechanic wasn't added to the game, and that, too, takes away the realism from the game. Something like, if you can't find something in the game that you're looking for, that's related to a certain character, search the appropriate term up, and find it (like [i]Her Story[/i]). That's what would make it more engaging, because there's no knowing what you could possibly find. Clicking and dragging can get stale. Hopefully, if they make a follow-up to [i]Orwell[/i], they could implement this.

In the sense of gameplay, it's pretty interesting. As you play, you come across multiple choices to make. You're basically making choices constantly. When you have an info that you have the choice of either using it or not, you will probably think of the following:

"Do I drag this information to the profile?"
"[i]Should[/i] I drag this information to the profile?"
"How does this information have an effect?"
"Is this info even worth putting into the files?"

A simple statement that has to do something with the character - you will think it about in a much deeper manner. Because when you do enter something, it gets reflected on the reports, and that could have a cause-and-effect thing going on. The "choices matter" tag on this game is appropriate. And that's the whole point of the game. You, as an investigator, must see to it that everything you do in this works out perfectly in the end, for the people in Orwell, as well as the public.

[h1]Music:[/h1]

The music fits well with the theme of the game, it's sci-fi-y, it gives off the mysterious vibe, and if you see a plot twist, the music suddenly changes to a very tense, "oh damn" type of tone. 

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]

If all you do in a game is walk, then you call it a "walking simulator". This game is that. All you mostly do is click and drag stuff. Which makes it a "clicking simulator". But, it's appropriate, because you can't really do much with a computer other than click and drag and type, can you? 

Funny (lol, not) jokes aside, the premise of the game is solid, and how they elaborate on it, with you as the very thing that gets to use what's given to you against those [b]like[/b] us. Just imagine if this happened ([b][i]*cough*ishappening*cough*[/i][/b]) in real life. The primary focus of the game was definitely the story, and the story only. The replayability of the game relies on the achievements, and the multiple endings present in the game (for most, even trading cards).

I recommend this game to story lovers, I don't recommend this game to those who get bored of simple mechanics, and I recommend you get this game during the sales. I enjoyed the story a lot, but, I wanted more to do than just clicking and dragging. There's a [i]f-i-i-i-ne[/i] grey area between those two, and I'm right smack in the middle of it. But, being a game that focuses entirely on the story, and the kind of message it's trying to interpret to us, I give it a thumbs up.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] An Excellent Educational Tool for Teaching People the Value of Privacy [/h1]

I am going to start this review with a hot take: people don't care much about privacy. At least not in the way we're taught to think about it. People desire privacy when they want to hide from others—especially people they know. A classic example of this is your average teenager concealing their sexual activity from their parents. We can define this as [b]interpersonal privacy[/b]—the need and right to keep parts of ourselves hidden from the people around us. In a limited sense, people do care about having (intepersonal) privacy  in their lives. 

But what about a faceless entity like a government agency or a big tech company? Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not.

Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided.

[list]
[*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it.
[*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens.
[*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list]

Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse.

Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy.

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2]
[list]
[*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women."
[*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps?
[*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps?
[*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism?
[/list]

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have.

[h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2]
Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! 

This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy!

Bottom line:  I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth!

[h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2]
Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with.

That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him!

[h2] Reading Haters [/h2]
Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle.

My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts.

[h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2]
Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that.

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%.

Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch!

My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements.

For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! 

[h1] Overall Rating [/h1]
[b] WIP, FIS, IIS
2+2=5/6 [/b]

You have the power to choose in Orwell! This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy! Bottom line: I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth! [h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2] Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with. That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him! [h2] Reading Haters [/h2] Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle. My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts. [h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2] Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that. [h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2] The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%. Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch! My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements. For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! [h1] Overall Rating [/h1] [b] WIP, FIS, IIS 2+2=5/6 [/b]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Excellent game.

To those who know the references and like the source material this game is based off of, this is perhaps the best Big Brother/Orwellian Surveillance system simulator I've seen so far, and is well worth the price its asking for. 

Fans of Papers, Please will probably enjoy this game just as much. Except instead of being the Border Crossing Guard, think of yourself as the Investigator for their Surveillance Corps.

Its a short game, sure, you can beat it once probably within 4 hours, but it does have some replayability (plus the fact that there is no hard save points, the game constantly saves after everything you do with no way of going back outside of making a new profile, so it forces you to choose wisely). To me, the shortness is forgiveable for how much this game costs (which isn't much).

The writing is amazing for it being a game with only written dialogue, the characters feel real and individual and you're the spider trying to weave out the web of how they fit into the plot that's going on. It also does a great job of getting you into the role of being an Investigator of a secret service public spying agency, you feel as if you're in the game just as much as any of them at times.

The art style is consistent and works for the game that this is, but IMO they could have had clear photos and models and you would have had the same game, this style merely gives it a more individual feel rather than it being like any other game like this.

The gameplay is simple, but great if you're into investigative puzzle-solving.

The music is very good for eliciting responses and making you feel certain emotions at particular times, as its supposed to, though IMO it moves a little too fast at times in transitions. You're often left with an abrupt music cue and wondering "What the hell, what did I just find?" before you can properly read what found. But otherwise its good.

Only encountered one bug at the very end of the game where it froze and looped the last second or two of the music track I was listening to, and I had to exit out with alt-tab, but I had beaten the playthrough by that point so it wasn't a huge deal.

All and all, a great game for the price its asking for, and if you're a fan of the type of genre this is.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Given all the positive reviews, I thought Orwell would be a more interesting game than it actually is.
But the gameplay is mostly boring. In a way, it is very similar to a text-adventure game. You read through/listen to all the documents given access to (webpages, chat sessions or phone calls). But there is basically no investigative work, hacking or anything that would be fun to do to find information. All the work is already done for you, every document is already analyzed, and you cannot investigate new people before being allowed to, even if it is clear they must have some role in the investigation.

So yes, the gameplay is overly simple and very linear, but maybe I could have been ok with it if I had found the story interesting.
But the story is boring. The main goal in the game (at least until I stopped playing) is to find the culprits responsible for a bomb attack. Sounds exciting right? Except most of the info you have to read through is about the different suspects boring life, relationships and habits, things I don't give a damn about. So I guess this game is not for me.

Maybe the game becomes more complex and interesting later on (I really hope so), but I am just not interested enough so far in the story to continue playing. Maybe I'll try again later...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This one's a "buy it only on sale" for me. I would pick a neutral option were it available.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Long story short: Great interactive [b]novel[/b]. Very addicting and compelling storytelling.

Long story ahead:
But, is this a game? And if it is a game what is the [i]enjoyment[/i] a player could have from playing it?

I have three main references as game definition:
[list]
[*][quote]Games are an exercise of voluntary control systems, in which there is a contest between powers, confined by rules in order to produce a disequilibrial outcome.
—Elliot Avedon and Brian Sutton-Smith[/quote]
[*][quote]A game is an interactive structure of endogenous meaning that requires players to struggle toward a goal.
—Greg Costikyan[/quote]
[*][quote]
A game is a closed, formal system, that engages players in structured conflict, and resolves in an unequal outcome.
—Tracy Fullerton, Chris Swain, and Steven Hoffman[/quote]
[/list]
Maybe you are questioning yourself why should I to struggle to classify Orwell as a game or as an interactive novel. The reply is really simple: because it changes a lot the review. And just because Orwell is very borderline I will review it twice, one review as an interactive novel and one as a game letting the reader to choose what fits best.

[b]Orwell as an interactive graphic novel[/b]
The story is really interesting and compelling, keeping you addicted to it until the end.

The novel is [i]pretty short[/i], I have walkthrough it twice in less than 11 hours, but when the storytelling is strong, able to immerse the reader, shortness is not an issue.

The music is nice, but a bit [i]repetitive[/i], above all when you hear mostly the same loop for hours, broken for short time by a drama loop.

Maybe this interactive novel is a bit too much expensive, but it is strongly suggested if you are able to get it on sale.


[b]Orwell as a game[/b]
Pros:
[list]
[*]Story
[/list]
Cons:
[list]
[*]Lack of choice and freedom
[*]Event based system and strong linear game, if you don't do what is expected the story does not go on
[*]Less than 8 hours of gameplay to get to the end (first time you play, otherwise a lot less)
[*]Max of 3-4 replays before having seen all what the game has to offer meaning less than 20/25 hours of total gameplay.
[*]Music: 1 main repetitive theme loop + some other drama stings...
[/list]

I am sorry but being this sold as a game I couldn't [b]honestly[/b] suggest to buy it, and anyway as I have already written as an interactive novel is a bit too much expensive.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell had me lost for words. Featuring a variety of references to George Orwell's dystopian political and surveillance novel, the game offered an interesting concept as to what may have been the beginning of Oceania. Of course this game has no canon with the novel that I happened to study in school just before discovering this game.

There is something extremely captivating about playing a game in which you dig into the most private aspects of the lives of several different characters. From the start, I was sure that there would be some revelation that you should not enter information that may harm the futures of these potentially dangerous characters but the actual plot twist featured at the end of the game was both unexpected and in a way poetic.

This game surpassed my expectations and with a beautiful soundtrack and imagery featured through-out this Papers, Please reminiscent game was captivating and extremely fun. I highly recommend it.

Notes: I played the first episode/demo for free before purchasing the game and playing all but one episode in one night (I would have played the final episode but I had to go to sleep for work the following morning).

review_text_raw:
"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" is an outstanding game that had me hooked from start to finish. The developers have masterfully crafted a gripping and unsettling story that tackles contemporary issues such as surveillance, privacy, and ethics.

The gameplay mechanics are unique and innovative. As a player, you take on the role of an investigator who sifts through data and analyzes information to uncover threats to national security. Throughout the game, you are faced with moral decisions that significantly impact the storyline. These choices are often challenging and thought-provoking, making the game a deeply engaging experience.

The atmosphere of the game is excellently executed. The visual design and soundtrack contribute to creating a dense and suspenseful mood. What is particularly impressive is how realistic and believable the world of "Orwell" feels. You truly feel like a part of this dystopian society.

Another highlight is the storytelling. The narrative is thrilling and full of twists that constantly surprise you. The characters are well-developed, and their fates are compelling. You quickly form an emotional connection with the characters and find yourself rooting for them.

Overall, "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" is a masterpiece that not only entertains but also makes you think. It is a game that stays with you long after you have finished playing. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an intelligent and captivating game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. 
After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. 
Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.”
Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.
Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.
