game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL - 3/10

Quick Review:  A slightly more interactive version of a visual novel, Orwell tries to claim some of the success legendary books like 1984 and Brave New World have. Unfortunately it's cliche and boring characters, simple and tedious gameplay, long wait times and confusing target audience make this a game I can't possibly recommend.

Story
-------
You play as an investigator who is hired from outside a country where a new system called "Orwell" is put in place. In it's early stages, Orwell is being used to collect data and spy on people in order to keep the public safe. After a bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza, your job is to find who is behind the bombing by investigating someone who has a small criminal history that was at the scene and see what you can discover from there.

The story isn't particularly interesting and while there are some major plot events I don't think they hit their intended mark for me because I wasn't particularly captivated in the first place. The characters you have to investigate are all the typical "fuck the government" protesters with little to no original personality traits. Everything is unoriginal and cliche as can be.

Gameplay
--------------
Orwell is split into 5 episodes, each taking roughly around 40 minutes to an hour. You sit in front of a virtual computer screen representing the UI for Orwell, and you have to drag and drop highlighted bits of information from various pages (news articles/blogs/websites etc) in order to learn more about the people you're investigating. Some of these bits will be conflicting (highlighted in yellow, like addresses or opinions). You will have to listen in on conversations, read personal emails. You're basically just spying on people and using their profiles to learn more about them.

The gameplay is literally just drag and drop information onto the character it is relevant too. You don't even actually need to read anything because all the important information will be highlighted anyway. Conflicting information is important because it defines what happens to each character at the end of an episode but it's always easy to figure out which is right once you discover what both conflicting elements are (which the game will tell you anyway once you find both). You'll also have to listen to long, unskippable and un-fastforwadable phone calls for a tiny bit of information.

Design
---------
I think the game interface, while basic does look nice. It's entirely pale blue and means that the game doesn't feel aggressive or heavy. The soundtrack is forgettable, I turned it down pretty early to help me concentrate. The writing is actually pretty good but the characters and story is just unoriginal.

Problems
-------------
The biggest problem is that it's just boring. There barely is anything that constitutes real gameplay as all you're doing is dragging + dropping or waiting around for phone calls to end. As the story isn't very interesting (to me anyway) the further I got into the game the more of a chore it became. As I also said, almost everything is a straight appropriation of the older Orwellian style novels. I mean the game is called "Orwell". I seriously also hated having to wait around and listen to phone calls. It would've been better for the characters to have the call offscreen and you just get uploaded the transcript once you collect enough information (so phone calls would act like checkpoints; like the rest of the articles in the game do).

Achievements
-------------------
As the gameplay is almost non-existant, all achievements are based on what you decide to upload to Orwell. In the first episode if you upload all the peaceful things related to the first target you'll get an achievement, but if you upload how she suffers from PTSD or hates the government you'll get another. You will have to play each episode at least twice (the third episode needs to be played 3 times). game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I am really conflicted on this game.
On one hand, it looks and sounds excellent, being extremely stylish and immersing the player into a dystopian world of total surveillence, the characters being (mostly) well-written and felt alive. All the websites, social networks, advertisement banners and the online banter is very realistic, they even included some made-up memes for their made-up world that looked like something that could actually exist in ours. Also, had a high-quality localisation to my native language (Russian) and i didn't really feel like i was missing anything out by not playing it in its original language.

Now, on the other hand. This game mostly play out like a visual novel, where you make your choices in whether or not to upload a certain bit of marked information into the system. There are also bits with "conflicting facts" in which you also can make a choice that can affect how will the story develop. And, for the most of the game, yor choices do matter: will a certain character go to jail or manage to escape the police? Will you frame someone who made a minor break of the law into something more incriminating, so he will actually get arrested? It is incredubly nice: as a player, you feel the real power of someone with the tools for total surveillence, with only your own morals that might prevent you from abusing that power. 
The story itself plays out nicely, keeping the player in suspence, with enough of "Oh god" moments to keep you invested... right until its final part. For me, it really felt like the game did a U-turn and started pushing its morals on me, instead of letting me, as a player, to make the final choice. Sure, there are multiple endings, but all of them mostly convey the same idea (no spoilers), which, i felt, was insulting to all the choices i made before it. I expected it to be more "morally-grey", especially considering how well it started, but in the end it tried to be a lesson in how you should think. And those very same people tell us about thought crimes? Ironic.

Not recommended, unless you are fine with the game's morale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a difficult one to critique because whether or not you like it is mainly dependent on whether you like the narrative and how it is told. I’m not going to pretend that I know a huge amount about a good story well told, so when it comes to my thoughts on said story, take them with a grain of salt. Before I discuss that though, let’s talk about the game a bit.

[h1]“Interactive” Story[/h1]

In context, you are supposed to be a sort of investigator searching for clues about persons of interest via their emails, social media feeds, and phone conversations. I wouldn’t use the word “investigate” to describe the gameplay. Every import piece of information is already highlighted for you and you just need to drag-and-drop them to the appropriate location. When it comes selecting which documents you want to search through, there are indicators that tell which ones have important data-chunks. You don’t really have to read through the documents and phone texts unless you want story context.

This does streamline the gameplay experience, though. With a lot of story based adventure or point-and-click games, there is a risk of getting stuck at one part and losing all immersion in indirection proportion to mounting frustration. Orwell doesn’t have this problem as it is always very clear where you are supposed to look and this keeps a smooth pacing. As I mentioned earlier, this does contribute to the whole experience not feeling much like a traditional game as it feels much more like a guided tour of the characters and narrative progression. Perhaps a system where you have to highlight pieces of text you feel are important, and if you got the right piece then the story could progress? That may have been the original idea, but that could lead to many frustrations if you just barely missed the part of a quote you were supposed to get.

The only real gameplay in here is when there are two pieces of data that conflict with each other and you have to decide which one to submit to your superior. This could come in the form of two phone conversations by a character where one conversation makes him sound violent and the other makes him sound peaceful. Which one you submit will determine if that character gets arrested later in the story. This factors into a bit of a moral choice system regarding whether you try to paint the main characters and virtuous activists or terrorists. I feel an opportunity was missed to have more greatly divergent storylines to make the player feel like they have a real impact on the world. As it stands, your decisions only change minor events and what ending you get, with most of the heavy decision making existing in the last episode only.

[h1]Interactive “Story”[/h1]

With everything I’ve had to say about the gameplay thus far, you may be a bit perplexed as to why I recommend Orwell. Once again, this isn’t a typical [i]game[/i]. It’s a story with a bit more user control over the pace at which you progress through it. So how is the story?

Pretty good, actually.

The subject matter: government surveillance, is very topical and the game does a good job of showing the many different angles and opinions that people have about it. From those that try to peacefully discuss the issue, publicly criticize it, or are indifferent to it, every character seems believable and for the most part are consistent. The plot is revealed at a steady pace and is able to constantly engage. Appropriate music cues help to reinforce when something drastic has just taken place or when a particularly important piece of data is discovered and it does a good job of drawing you in. The last episode starts to deteriorate when the story starts to massively diverge and the amount of documents and computers to search through becomes overwhelming compared to the rest of the story.

While the data chunks are the most important piece of the story, there is a lot of text to sift through and it fleshes out the characters and game world quite well. A lot of it is unnecessary and for a while I thought that a small sub-plot about terrorism in another country was going to turn out to be a major plot device because the game kept bringing it up, but that ended up being nothing important. Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator.

There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing. [h1]Performance[/h1] Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that I have mixed feeling about. While I did enjoy the game, I also want to clarify that there is certainly more than one issue with the game that makes me want to not recommend it.

The gameplay boils down to one and only one mechanic. Being able to drag selected text into a profile which affects the story. You need to bounce between internet pages, phone-call logs, and a few other forms of data to find keywords and important text to upload. Depending on what you upload, what the government believes and what happens to the person(s) involved changes. Do you portray a spoiled brat as a terrorist? An old man as a kind teacher. You decide what information they've put online defines them, very literally. 

The issues I have with this is as such: 
[olist]
    [*]Choices don't ultimately matter.
    [*]It is painfully short.
    [*]A lack of any audio design.
[/olist]

From top to bottom, the linearity of the game. Despite being able to chose what information does or doesn't get uploaded, a lot (and I do mean a LOT) of events will happen regardless of your actions. The game literally says in it's description: "But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." However, despite this, the only things my choices ended up affecting were the achievements. And spoiler alert: [spoiler] You can get any of the three endings no matter what choices you made in previous episodes. [/spoiler] Sure, on a superficial surface level your choices have consequences, but these "consequences" never actually impact your story or gameplay expericence.

Onto the next, the length. You may see me having 7.5 hours and tell me "Oh well 7.5 hours in NOT a short game!" You'd be right. Except Orwell is not 7.5 hours long, it is 3 hours long at most and 2 hours long at it's shortest. The only reason I have more than 3 hours of playtime is because I went back to get all of the achievements, which is also why i know how little your choices affect the story. I've seen all the endings, seen the affect of almost all of the choices, and even then with some time spent idle I was able to see 99% of this game's offerings in under 8 hours. This isn't inherently bad, but Orwell has little to no gameplay, audio design, or anything. It's just an on rails story, and for it to be that short for a $10 USD price tag is a little much.

Lastly, the audio design. As previously mentioned, there is little to no audio in this game. You have 3 music tracks, the main menu theme, the basic ambient theme and a more intense theme for when things "get serious." Outside of the music, you might have a few computer beeps or a quick musical tone at random points, but they're so spread out that a majority of your time is spent with almost nothing going into your ears. You can't hear people on their phone calls, your boss can't speak to you, there are no audio transcripts. It is the most barebones audio design I've seen in a story driven game.

The only really good thing I'd argue in favor of is the art style. It is a fractal/cubism artstyle that absolutely draws you in. The issue is that this art style is not the primary focus, instead that focus is on a painfully bland UI. If you look at the screenshots on the store page, you see that profile tab on the right, your bar up top and the righthand screen? That is 90% of the game. Just looking at those screens It could've been so much more.

I really like the idea of Orwell, an Orwellian (pun not intended) dystopia with a spying government and terrorist plots. The thing that makes me not like it though is literally everything else about it. And that is the problem.

Struggled a bit on the choice - and then lean towards not recommending. 

Considering the time when the game was published, the core mechanism could be quite creative at that time. And I get the idea that this game is trying to discuss the debate behind freedom in words, personal privacies and safety & threat monitoring - but the angle it cuts into makes really non-sense. These guys are just terrorists - the way they protect their freedom is through bombing the busy places and killing innocent citizens... And giving me the choice to forgive them makes also nonsence. At the end, they still don't realize their problems. This makes the whole argument meaningless. [/spoiler]

I have to say that maybe judging a game with a perspective after 10 years does not sound fair, but there are classic games that can be lifelong legend. Unfortunately, this game does not  reach this level.

review_text_raw:
In this game, you play as a special government agent, who's job is to make your country secure from terrorists. 

The game is divided into 5 episodes, there are 2 episodes released as of the time of writing. Each episode is a "day" at work. When investigating, you search through data on the virtual "internet", which is full of interesting things to explore and read, both important to your mission and fillers.

Graphics are simple, clean and very easy to look at.

Sounds are simple, no voice acting present (unfortunately).

Music is ambient, mostly relaxing, when things happen it gets much more energetic, adding to the atmosphere.

Throughout the game you work with your co-worker Symes. He has interesting insight into the problems at hand and is generaly not intrusive - leaving the problem solving to you which is excelent.

The main thing - the Story is very interesting. It is just exciting enough and believeable enough, that you can really dive deep into it. Each character has it's backstory and is written very well.

Overall, I think this game is absolutely worth the EUR 10 price. It's fun, interesting and get's you thinking. They could easily make this into a "season" game, releasing 5-6 episode in a season for 5-10 bucks every now and then.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A wonderful game.

Have you played a Telltale game recently? Do you notice that most of your decisions are cosmetic or mere distractions except for the one or two major decisions? You probably have thought about that. There are a number of different reactions to this fact. Either the games are so interesting you just don't notice/care (Walking Dead), you're willing to let it slide (The Wolf Among Us), or it absolutely spoils the game by making the player feel powerless (Game of Thrones).

What if there could be a game that took into account every decision the player made and changed the plot accordingly?

Orwell does this. In a way that is sometimes overwhelming.

The premise of the game is somewhat reminiscent of Papers, Please. You are hired as a government worker. Your job is to be connected to a massive spy-network which has access to the entire internet and can bypass all privacy settings. You're tasked with investigating a terrorist incident, finding suspects, and hopefully stopping their plans before they happen.

You cannot directly decide what or who to investigate. What you do is you highlight certain passages you uncover (from people's blogs, text messages, phone conversations, etc) and submit them to the system, which will then build its case in the direction the evidence will go. One of the first conflicts you're given to resolve is the investigation of a young woman who is a political activist. One who writes on her political essays "We are dedicated to peaceful means to promote political change," and then writes on her personal blog in a fit of anger: "DEATH TO ALL WHO DISAGREE WITH US!"

Do you submit the intellectual and rational example in an attempt to give the subject the benefit of the doubt, or do you decide the words spoken emotionally are her true feelings?

If you're getting the impression the game is meant to be a parable about the futility of massive surveilance and how invasive it is, there's one problem with that assessment: it's possible to actually succeed and prevent crimes this way.

The game gives the player a lot of credit in this respect. They don't settle for a straightforward storyline with a didactic message. There are certainly messages conveyed about surveillance and its implementation, how it affects people, etc., but the game's storyline is genuinely about the characters and the environment they're in, not a tract about politics.

If the gameplay sounds boring, be assured in that the game actually manages to make many scenes genuinely tense and thrilling as well. You will scramble to acquire more datachunks before time runs out and genuinely panic at some points.

It's a truly great experience, well worth the price, and I heartily recommend it because it really does make it feel like every choice you make, every little bit of data you feed to this huge system that guides the investigation really does matter.

Though there is one low point which I'll discuss. It involves some spoilers, so stop reading if you want to avoid them.


***spoilers***


The most conflicting thing about this game is its ending. Specifically there are three different types of endings with some variations between them. Just finished this beautiful, beautiful game.

I can't say enough good things about it. From the subtle and gorgeous music, to the crisp and stylized artwork, to the streamlined "browser" interface of the game design, to the brilliant and immersive writing... this game is just a work of art.

If you're a fan of "decisions matter" games, especially ones with a "human vs. government" aspect like "Papers, Please", or if you're just in the mood for what's essentially a gorgeous interactive novel, you need this game. As other reviewers have said, don't watch gameplay vids, don't read about the story, just play it. It's worth the money.

It's been a long time since a game captured me so completely. The twists and turns and gradual unwinding of the plot happen at such a perfect pace. There were times I burst out laughing, times I was actually brought to tears, and even half a chapter where I sat with one hand over my mouth as I clicked through with the other. Now I can't wait to play it again to make different choices and see how things play out.

10/10 would happily subject myself to emotional battery again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

review_text_raw:
If you like games with a lot of actual gameplay this isn't for you. But if you like story-driven, psychological thrillers that keep you guessing, you're in for a treat. 

The UI and art style is extremely crisp and surprisingly uncluttered considering the amount of stuff you constantly have to click through. Articles and conversations are well-written, and the characters have a lot of personality.

The music/sound is minimal, but the game does a great job of using it to increase drama during major discoveries.

Story is really good, by far the highlight of the game. Without spoiling anything, there are lots of twists that you don't really see coming. And I have to say, the game manages to get a lot of emotion into a game with no voice acting. You really do start to feel for some of these characters at times. 

Overall, if you really like this type of game it will be worth $10. It is short (I've beaten it in about 4.5 hours) but it never feels like it's dragging on to the point where I just wish it would end. It's just solid action from start to finish. One of my favorite games of 2016.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one. [h1] Other: [/h1] The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end. The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short. [h1] TL:DR: [/h1] If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal. Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth. -Thanks for reading -Cain

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I believe Fellow Traveller Games is very interested in making people switch to Tails with giving away their published "Linux basics" game Hacknet for free (multiple times even!) first, and now give away this game too to fuel your paranoia and use some of that know-how to make you try and hide.

Tin foil hat aside, here's a proper review;

First a little disclaimer, not recommended if you use a monitor smaller than 1080p, especially if you have an unusual aspect ratio too.
The font in some spots looks terrible, occasionally skipping through thinner letters like i's and l's altogether and overall making the rest harder to read, notably the whole TNB stuff aside the headlines.
There is no way to change the font neither through options nor through config files, forum searches gave nothing in regards to that either, so be mindful of that.

Firstly this is a visual novel, so no super exciting and engaging gameplay is to be found, but honestly that may be for the better in these spying games.

I have played a little bit of Beholder and the more involving gameplay was a huge turn off due to how boring the whole manually keep track of data part already is, and Beholder also puts you on a timer and penalizes you for messing up by submitting wrong data for the whole accountant simulator part, and that is not counting the other gameplay aspects like resource management, relationships with people and quests and the overall keeping track of who is where part in the house sections. Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story.
But if you like these spying games and want one focused on gameplay, go and check out Beholder instead.

Otherwise if a more streamlined experience suits you better, proceed with this review.
Firstly, I'm not a Visual Novel expert, this one is my first one that wasn't completely linear, so the bar was set very low with the few ones I've played being just click proceed until all of the text scrolls past. Well this one has proper branching patchs and dfferent endings and little optional side stuff too. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough.

You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three.
You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel.
At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue.

Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc.

I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot.
But turns out the sequel actually plays alongside the original with focus on that foreign affairs story with the bombings plot of the original serving as a backdrop helping you keep track of the time.

Overall I'd say the game is fun, you won't get more than 18 hours out of it even if you 100% it, so I don't know at what price you should get it if you missed he free promo.
The sequel seems promising though, and there's also the whole movie shooting actor/director feud in the news much like the war, so trilogy potential?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just picked Orwell up in the sale, thought it looked interesting. It was. VERY. 
The game's premise is a controversial one, and one that could merit debate for hours, and it explores this concept well, on multiple situations. The morality of what you, and ultimately the people you're working against do is questioned numerous times. 

If however, you're not looking at a question of ethics, I'd still reccomend this game, although a tad on the short side (I completed it in under 6 hours), the story and game content is fun and gets you really thinking. Having to filter information and disregarding things said out of context instead of just dragging and dropping everything in was a nice touch. The gameplay is solid, the visuals are ok, the music is good and builds atmosphere. All in all, a good game.

I only hope that they add more cases, even as a DLC, otherwise once you have played through the game once, the gripping story would certainly lose its charm.

TL:DR - Good solid game, limited replayability, short completion time. Hoping for more content. Worth £5 from the sale.
